comment.value:
This paper introduces a new benchmark consisting of drone-captured videos for aerial anomaly understanding tasks. Some concerns have been raised by the reviewers about the relevance of the collected dataset, especially in comparison to other benchmarks such as UCFC, XD-Violence, etc. (although those benchmarks are mostly collected in a viseo-surveillance scenario). Reviewer ZhtC raised also concerns about missing comparisons to aerial-specific baselines.

The authors did a very good job in their rebuttal, and all the major concerns have been adequately addressed. In the discussion phase all the reviewers were satisfied by the authors' responses and all the reviewers recommended acceptance in their final review (two of them raised the original recommendation from BR to A). The area chair shares their opinion and strongly encourages the authors to include the material presented in the rebuttal phase in their camera ready.

author_final_remarks.value:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive and insightful feedback, and are pleased to have addressed all concerns to their satisfaction.

During the rebuttal, we clarified the design and novelty of GoT with concrete annotation examples and clearer implementation details (W3fo, 41Bh); added analyses of speed and stability; validated A2Seek-R1 on broader base models; and providing concrete explanations and analysis of its effectiveness and generalization performance (W3fo, umRr); expanded benchmarking to include aerial-specific baselines and diverse large-scale VAD datasets (ZhtC, umRr); emphasized dataset diversity and label quality with detailed scene coverage, class balance analysis, anomaly definition justification, and inter-annotator agreement (ZhtC, umRr); and explained key-frame selection and handling of long-duration anomalies for temporal localization (41Bh).

In addition, we greatly appreciate and are encouraged by the reviewers' unanimous recognition that:

**Our work is important and impactful**

- "A2Seek will facilitate the development of aerial anomaly understanding." - W3fo
- "...the largest and most diverse aerial anomaly detection dataset..." - umRr
- "...enable robust reasoning and precise anomaly localization in complex aerial video scenarios." - ZhtC
- "It fills the gap in this field and shows diversity..., making it a valuable contribution." - 41Bh

**Our dataset is diverse and well-constructed**

- "...covers various scenarios and environmental conditions, providing high-resolution real-world aerial videos with detailed annotations..." - W3fo
- "...with complex scene variations, fine-grained annotations..." - umRr
- "...enabling anomaly detection under diverse visibility conditions, including nighttime and occlusion." - ZhtC
- "...the first large-scale dataset in this domain, covering diverse anomaly types, scenarios, and weather conditions." - 41Bh

**Our method is novel and effective**

- "...a novel reasoning framework that generalizes R1-style strategies to aerial anomaly understanding." - W3fo
- "...a novel two-stage approach tailored for aerial anomaly detection." - ZhtC
- "...a novel seeking mechanism that simulates UAV flight behavior to dynamically focus on critical regions." - umRr
- "...improving both reasoning ability and spatial localization." - 41Bh

Finally, we express our sincere gratitude to the Area Chair for the thoughtful guidance and support, which have greatly contributed to improving this work.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the novelty of our work (`"It fills the gap in this field"`), the contribution of our dataset (`"covering diverse anomaly types, scenarios, and weather conditions"`), and the effectiveness of our method (`"This design improves both reasoning ability and spatial localization"`). 

We have carefully considered your constructive suggestions and provide point-by-point responses to address your specific concerns:

> **Q1-(i): Why GoT over CoT or video descriptions?**

Unlike CoT or video descriptions, which follow a linear narrative structure, GoT decomposes reasoning into multiple optional semantic stages (Trigger → Diagnose → Reasoning → Reflection → Seeking). This allows for flexible, dynamic connections between stages, enabling a more realistic, human-like reasoning process capable of handling complex logical relationships, such as branching and feedback.

Aerial scenes often present large viewpoint changes, occlusions, and diverse environmental conditions. GoT allows the model to adjust its reasoning depth based on scene complexity, making it more effective than fixed-length chains in handling subtle anomalies (e.g., falls under occlusion) and straightforward ones (e.g., visible fighting).

GoT provides more structured and hierarchical supervision by using phase-specific annotations, guiding the model to learn key reasoning paths. This leads to stronger generalization and interpretability compared to CoT or video descriptions. A comparative study on the A2Seek benchmark shows that GoT improves anomaly detection performance, raising the AP from 31.10% to 46.42%, validating its advantage in handling complex aerial anomalies.

| Method |AP (%)|Δ AP (%)|mIoU (%)|Δ mIoU (%)|
|-|-|-|-|-|
|ANS|31.10|-|12.13|-|
|CoT|38.24|+7.14|17.05|+4.92|
|GoT|46.42|+8.18|20.81|+3.76|

>  **Q1-(ii): How is GoT implemented**?

Graph-of-Thought (GoT) models the reasoning process by injecting structured language tags, i.e., <|Trigger|>, <|Diagnose|>, <|Reasoning|>, <|Reflection|>, and <|Seeking|>, into the target sequence. These tags define a semantically staged, adjustable reasoning path that guides the model to interpret anomalies in a structured and interpretable way.

Each GoT stage is skippable, allowing the model to dynamically adjust reasoning depth based on input complexity, operating efficiently in simple scenarios, such as an empty playground, while expanding into deeper reasoning for more complex situations, such as aerial imagery with varying object scales, frequent occlusions, and background distractions.

During the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage, semantic tags are injected into the model's output sequence and jointly optimized under a unified objective. This supervision encourages the model to learn multi-stage reasoning patterns. In the reinforcement learning (RL) stage, no hard constraints are imposed on the reasoning path. Instead, rewards are assigned based on the accuracy of the final output, guiding the model to explore the best reasoning strategy for each scene.

Upon closer inspection, there is no direct indication of the person interacting with the lawn itself, such as stepping onto it. Instead, the focus shifts to the possibility of a lost item, as the person's movement does not suggest any abnormal interaction with the environment beyond walking.",

"reflection": "Given the lack of direct interaction with the lawn and the person's adherence to the pathway, the most plausible explanation is that the person has dropped an item. This aligns with the category 'Lost Item', as the person's movement pattern does not suggest trespassing but rather a search for something they may have misplaced.",

> **Q2-(i): The discussion of temporal localization.**

We appreciate the reviewer's recognition of our contributions to spatial localization and frame-level reasoning, which are central to aerial anomaly detection. Temporal localization is also explicitly addressed during dataset construction, where each anomaly is annotated with precise start and end frames.

During inference, A2Seek-R1 processes clips using a sliding-window approach and outputs anomaly scores for each. These scores are concatenated along the timeline to identify anomalous intervals. We have clarified this procedure in the revised manuscript and included temporal visualizations in both the main text and appendix to illustrate the model's predictions over time.



> **Q2-(ii): How are key frames selected?**

We follow the preprocessing steps used in XD-Violence and LAVAD. First, all videos undergo uniform frame extraction, selecting every 16th frame from the original stream, resulting in approximately 155k extracted frames. During the manual annotation, we classify the segments as abnormal or normal. Abnormal frames are retained as long as they are not excessively blurred and the subject remains identifiable, resulting in 19,792 abnormal frames (79.45% of the total). To address class imbalance, we randomly retain 9.56% of the normal frames, yielding 12,972 normal frames.

Due to memory constraints, we combine every 4 consecutive frames into a clip, with the last frame serving as the "key frame" during prediction. These clips are sequentially fed into the model using a sliding window approach. The model generates anomaly scores and GoT inferences for each clip, and the results are concatenated along the time axis to form the final prediction. The "key frame" is implicitly defined as the last frame of each 4-frame clip during prediction, based on a fixed extraction and segmentation strategy, without any additional selection mechanism.

Nevertheless, the sliding-window inference strategy generates repeated predictions over time, forming a continuous anomaly score trajectory that offers coarse temporal coverage.

To further improve temporal modeling, we plan to adopt overlapping windows with lightweight memory mechanisms such as temporal attention, and to design fine-grained discriminators and efficient frame selection strategies that enhance the model's ability to capture semantic continuity over extended durations.

Moreover, we note that existing aerial anomaly detection datasets (e.g., Drone-Anomaly, AU-AIR-Anomaly) generally provide only binary labels at the segment level or coarse-grained timestamps, without precise spatial boundaries or causal explanations. Under such settings, models tend to rely on local motion surges and make "instant alert"-style predictions, limiting their ability to learn cross-frame logic or verify evidence chains. Both ANDT and HSTforU are developed under this paradigm, with a focus on salient motion regions or optical flow features. As a result, they struggle with complex scenarios such as environmental occlusion, weak visual signals, or multi-agent interactions.

In contrast, our dataset offers frame-level temporal annotations, spatial bounding boxes of abnormal regions, and multi-stage semantic labels, enabling stronger structured supervision. This provides the foundation for A2Seek-R1 to model causal chains across frames, control its reasoning trajectory, and perform active verification. These capabilities allow it to excel in more challenging UAV-based anomaly understanding tasks. We have included these comparisons and clarifications in §5.2 and Table 2 of the revised version to thoroughly address the reviewer's concern.

> **Q2: Scene diversity and generalization.**

Diversity and representativeness are central to the design of A2Seek. While all data was collected within a university campus, we emphasize that scene diversity is systematically constructed through three key strategies: semantic sub-scene partitioning, multi-condition environmental modeling, and dynamic UAV trajectory variation. Additionally, the dataset incorporates an explicit generalization evaluation protocol to assess model robustness under complex distribution shifts.

First, in terms of spatial structure, A2Seek covers 27 semantically distinct sub-scenes across three separate campus zones, including intersections, rooftops, wall edges, stair entrances, parking lots, open plazas, and green boundaries. These sub-scenes span a wide range of spatial layouts and behavioral contexts, reflecting both enclosed and open spaces as well as static and dynamic environments. This design simulates urban-level semantic heterogeneity and captures the type of scene variation commonly encountered in real-world deployments.

Second, the dataset spans all four seasons, multiple times of day (daytime, evening, night), and diverse weather conditions such as clear, cloudy, rainy, and foggy. UAV flights were conducted with varying altitudes, speeds, and paths (e.g., circling, traversing, hovering), resulting in substantial visual variability even within the same location. This setting creates perceptual variation under constant semantics, which presents more realistic and challenging distribution shifts than geographic relocation alone.

Third, compared to existing aerial anomaly datasets such as Drone-Anomaly and AU-AIR-Anomaly, A2Seek provides more comprehensive annotations, including frame-level timestamps, bounding-box spatial labels, and structured reasoning chains (Trigger → Diagnose → Reasoning → Reflection → Seeking). These enable the study of cross-frame reasoning, evidence localization, causal inference, and decision-level uncertainty, which are not supported by coarse segment-level labels used in prior datasets.

We also provide a comparison with widely used ground-view datasets such as ShanghaiTech and NWPU Campus, as shown in the table below. This further illustrates that A2Seek is designed not for traditional classification or detection, but for fine-grained modeling of anomaly causality, temporal dynamics, and spatial localization in aerial video understanding.

In addition, we explicitly define In-Domain (ID) and Out-of-Domain (OOD) splits in our experimental setup. In contrast, A2Seek-R1 maintains steady and even improved performance on the OOD test set. This improvement is primarily attributed to our systematic scene diversity design at the dataset level and the method’s ability to model multiple reasoning paths across heterogeneous aerial scenes. > **Q3: Annotation consistency and quality control**.

We appreciate the reviewer's suggestion, which allowed us to present our annotation quality control more explicitly. A2Seek employs a three-annotator protocol for temporal labeling: the first two annotators independently annotate the start and end frames of video anomalies without visibility of each other's results, thereby avoiding subjective interference. A third annotator only intervenes when there is a disagreement (e.g., if the difference between the start and end frames exceeds 10 frames or if the event type is inconsistent). The third annotator, serving as the senior annotation lead, is blind to which result belongs to which of the first two annotators. Their judgment is based entirely on the video content and the annotation guidelines, rather than favoring any specific annotator's results. In fact, this lead annotator is also the primary developer of our annotation standards, possessing greater judgment and experience. It is important to note that most discrepancies are concentrated on the detailed calibration of the start and end frames, rather than the event type itself. The consistency of event categorization is very high. In cases of disagreement, the third annotator revisits the context and reviews the video segment from multiple angles to ensure a more rigorous and reliable final result. Consistency statistics show that the agreement rate between the first two annotators is 87.3%. For the remaining 12.7% of samples with discrepancies, the third annotator chose annotator A's result 56.2% of the time and annotator B's result 43.8%, indicating that the review process shows no systematic bias.

> **Q4: Huggingface image viewer displays incomplete images**.

The issue with incomplete image display in Huggingface's viewer was due to our initial upload method. We first uploaded image files in packaged formats, but Huggingface's default viewer only shows a limited number of images, which caused only the first few to be visible, missing the full range of scenes and modalities in our dataset.

We have updated our upload method to a distributed, small-file direct upload approach, allowing more images to be directly loaded and displayed by Huggingface. The current version now supports a more comprehensive image preview.

|Aspect|CoT-RAG|Our GoT|
|-|-|-|
|Meaning of the graph|Knowledge graph|Reasoning path graph|
|Nodes|Entities / Retrieved facts|Stages of reasoning (Trigger, Diagnose, Reasoning, Reflection, Seeking)|

Specifically, GoT introduces a structured reasoning path in the form of a graph, decomposing the reasoning process into multiple explicit steps. This design enables the model not only to detect anomalous events but also to progressively infer their causes and precise locations. Finally, in the *reflection* stage, the model infers that the individual may be searching for a dropped item, aligning best with the "Lost Item" category. To confirm, it initiates a *seeking* operation over region [270, 170, 582, 447], allowing the model to verify object presence and refine the spatial decision.

This example highlights how A2Seek-R1 performs structured, adaptive reasoning even under weak visual cues. RFT further refines this behavior by teaching the model to query additional context, improving decision reliability. This is reflected in the +6.72% AP and +5.22% mIoU improvement over GoT-SFT, demonstrating its superiority in both detection and localization.


> **Q5-(i): Reasoning Speed and Stability.**

Following your suggestion, we report a comparative analysis of inference speed, output token length, and scene-wise performance stability across different methods. All experiments are conducted on a single A100 GPU with FP16 precision. 
A2Seek-R1 achieves the best trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, reaching the highest AP (53.14%) while maintaining a reasonable inference speed (0.3267 sample/s). It also shows strong stability across diverse scenes, outperforming the zero-shot baseline by +6.29% (Miscellaneous), +7.70% (Park), +18.80% (Rooftop), and +16.30% (Academic Building).

|Zero-shot|34.03|0.6097|-|-|-|-|
|ANS-SFT|30.09|0.9174|-36.96|-02.37|-18.80|-13.33|
|GoT-SFT|46.42|0.2890|+04.61|+04.04|+04.00|+14.18|
|A2Seek-R1|53.14|0.3267|+06.29|+07.70|+18.80|+16.30|

> **Q5-(ii):** **Performance Comparison under Different Weather Conditions.**

We considered the impact of weather conditions during dataset construction, as they present significant challenges for aerial-view anomaly detection. As shown below, AP drops under foggy and nighttime conditions, while the model remains robust under cloudy and rainy weather, achieving APs of 61.48% and 60.49%, respectively. Notably, AP under sunny conditions is slightly lower (55.63%) than cloudy, likely due to glare or strong shadows affecting recognition. Under night conditions, mIoU drops sharply to 6.16% due to poor illumination, which weakens contextual cues and impairs localization accuracy. Since A2Seek includes both RGB and infrared modalities, future work can leverage infrared inputs to improve anomaly detection performance under such low-light conditions.

|Weather Condition|Sunny|Cloudy|Overcast|Rain|Foggy|Night|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
|AP(%)|55.63|61.48|51.55|60.49|42.37|45.36|
|mIoU (%)|31.04|21.76|23.53|19.20|14.15|06.16|

> **Q6: Why does the OOD generalization of COT-SFT rise at range [800-1000]?**

The temporary rise is due to the learning rate schedule. At higher rates, the model overfits to scene-specific background patterns. Around step 800, the decaying rate stabilizes training and encourages learning of structured reasoning cues in CoT, leading to a short-term boost in OOD generalization. As the rate continues to drop, the model gradually overfits to in-domain data again, causing OOD performance to decline. To illustrate this trend, we report results beyond step 800 in the table below.

|Step|A2Seek-R1|Δ AP(%)|GoT-SFT|Δ AP(%)|
|-|-|-|-|-|
|800|50.98|-|42.46|-|
|1000|51.12|+0.14|41.59|-0.87|
|1200|51.55|+0.43|41.14|-0.45|

> **Q7: The effectiveness of A2Seek-R1 on a broader base models.**

We integrated A2Seek-R1 into two additional models beyond the original QwenVL-2.5-3B: a larger QwenVL-2.5-7B with the same architecture, and a compact InternVL-3.0-2B with a different one. Results show that A2Seek-R1 consistently yields stable and significant performance gains across both model scales and architectures.

|Method|AP|Δ AP(%)|mIoU|Δ mIoU(%)|
|-|-|-|-|-|
|QwenVL-2.5-7B-Instruct|44.65|-|08.24|-|
|w/ A2Seek-R1|57.07|+12.42|29.71|+21.47|
|InertnVL-3.0-2B-Instruct|20.03|-| 00.10|-|
|w/ A2Seek-R1|48.76|+28.73|18.89|+18.79|

On the larger QwenVL-2.5-7B-Instruct, incorporating A2Seek-R1 leads to a 12.42% increase in AP and a 21.47% increase in mIoU, indicating its potential to further exploit the capacity of larger models. Meanwhile, on the smaller and more lightweight InertnVL-3.0-2B-Instruct, A2Seek-R1 still achieves substantial improvements, raising AP from 20.03% to 48.76% and mIoU from 0.10% to 18.89%. These results further verify the strong generalization ability of A2Seek-R1 across models of different scales and architectures, highlighting its robustness and transferability by design.

Then, they propose A2Seek (Aerial Anomaly Seek), a large-scale, reasoning-centric benchmark dataset for aerial anomaly understanding. strengths_contributions.value:
1. The issue of anomaly detection is clear. 
2. The problems of the existing dataset for anomaly detection are important; they will significantly affect the performance.
3. A2Seek (Aerial Anomaly Seek) is a big dataset in the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs)  way, for example, I found the author provides a dataset (Certain Region for Each Anomaly.zip) about 30.7 GB in Hugging Face. This dataset covers various scenarios and environmental conditions, providing high-resolution real-world aerial videos with detailed annotations, including anomaly categories, frame-level timestamps, region-level bounding boxes, and natural language explanations for causal reasoning. A2Seek will facilitate the development of aerial anomaly understanding.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The author should provide relevant theoretical analysis and experiments to prove their hypothesis. For example, in section 4, the author introduced their method, the main idea is based on Graph-of-Thought (GoT). However, Graph-of-Thought is not a new thing, i.e., “CoT-RAG: Integrating Chain of Thought and Retrieval-Augmented Generation to Enhance Reasoning in Large Language Models”. In addition, the author states their method can improve the reasoning capabilities on A2Seek, why? This statement should provide an in-depth analysis and theoretical validation.
2. I recommend thoroughly revising this paper, improving the clarity and the reader’s understanding. For example, I found that the samples provided by the author in some of the datasets provided by Huggingface are inconsistent with the analysis in the actual paper. For example, in Huggingface, most of the pictures are on the playground, and the video frames are very similar to each other. This misleads readers' understanding of the paper.
3. There exist some typos/grammatical errors in the paper that should be revised.

summary.value: This paper introduces A2Seek, a large-scale, reasoning-centric aerial anomaly detection benchmark. A2Seek provides drone-captured videos with complex scene variations, fine-grained annotations including anomaly categories, frame-level timestamps, region-level bounding boxes, and natural language causal reasoning. This paper proposes A2Seek-R1, a multi-stage reinforcement fine-tuning framework that integrates graph-of-thought reasoning and a novel seeking mechanism that simulates UAV flight behavior to dynamically focus on critical regions.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Proposes A2Seek, the largest and most diverse aerial anomaly detection dataset, providing not only spatial and temporal anomaly labels but also causal reasoning in natural language
- Introduces A2Seek-R1, which combines supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with graph-of-thought structured annotations.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The paper does not compare its performance against complex and diverse real-world video anomaly detection benchmarks such as UCFC [1], XD-Violence [2], UBI-Fight [3], LAD [4] and TAD [5]. These datasets often feature a greater variety of scenes, behaviors, and real-world challenges. A direct comparison, including scene counts, anomaly types, and frame statistics, would strengthen the argument for A2Seek’s practical relevance.

- Although the dataset is large, scene diversity appears limited compared to urban, traffic, or surveillance-heavy datasets commonly used in VAD literature. Methods trained on A2Seek may not generalize to diverse urban or densely populated real-world settings. The authors should discuss potential strategies to overcome this limitation, such as leveraging transfer learning or dataset fusion.

- Similar to many video anomaly detection datasets, A2Seek suffers from class imbalance between normal and abnormal frames, which seems more severe here given the small proportion of anomaly-containing frames relative to the total dataset size. It is unclear whether this trade-off between diversity and imbalance is justifiable or if it hinders the model’s ability to learn minority categories effectively. The imbalance across abnormal categories is also not sufficiently analyzed.

- Some labeled anomalies, such as “running,” “animal,” and “bicycle,” are ambiguous and may not be universally perceived as anomalous in real-world aerial monitoring. The authors do not sufficiently justify their anomaly selection criteria, raising concerns about the ecological validity of the abnormal class definitions.

- Although the UAV simulation and reasoning mechanisms are novel, the paper does not clearly address how the method would scale to highly complex and diverse real-world scenes beyond campus environments.

[1] Sultani, Waqas, Chen Chen, and Mubarak Shah. "Real-world anomaly detection in surveillance videos." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2018.
[2] Wu, Peng, et al. "Not only look, but also listen: Learning multimodal violence detection under weak supervision." Computer Vision–ECCV 2020: 16th European Conference, Glasgow, UK, August 23–28, 2020, Proceedings, Part XXX 16. Springer International Publishing, 2020.
[3] Degardin, Bruno, and Hugo Proença. "Iterative weak/self-supervised classification framework for abnormal events detection." Pattern Recognition Letters 145 (2021): 50-57.
[4] Wan, Boyang, et al. "Anomaly detection in video sequences: A benchmark and computational model." IET Image Processing 15.14 (2021): 3454-3465.
[5] Lv, Hui, et al. "Localizing anomalies from weakly-labeled videos." IEEE transactions on image processing 30 (2021): 4505-4515.

summary.value: A2Seek Introduces a large-scale aerial anomaly detection benchmark with fine-grained annotations including spatiotemporal labels, bounding boxes, and natural language reasoning traces. It uses Graph-of-Thought (GoT) supervised fine-tuning to guide models through structured reasoning stages (trigger, diagnosis, reasoning, reflection, seeking). Additionally, a customized reinforcement learning method (A-GRPO) introduces rewards for localization, seeking, and response conciseness, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability. Together, these components enable robust reasoning and precise anomaly localization in complex aerial video scenarios.

strengths_contributions.value:
1) A2Seek contains over 2.4 million frames captured across 23 hours of UAV footage using a drone with wide-angle, telephoto, and infrared sensors, enabling anomaly detection under diverse visibility conditions, including nighttime and occlusion. The dataset spans 27 sub-scene types with detailed spatiotemporal anomaly labels, bounding boxes, and natural language reasoning paths, providing rich context for semantic understanding.

2) The A2Seek-R1 framework introduces a novel two-stage approach tailored for aerial anomaly detection. It combines Graph-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning for structured reasoning, a reinforcement method using task-specific rewards. A key innovation is the “seeking” mechanism, which simulates UAV behavior by directing attention to regions needing further inspection

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1) In Table 2, all baseline methods evaluated were originally designed for ground-view anomaly detection. Although the authors cite aerial-specific methods (e.g., ANDT [24], HSTforU [26]) in Section 2 (Related Work), they do not benchmark against them. This limits the validity of performance claims, as improvements may partly reflect the mismatch between baseline models and the aerial task rather than superiority of A2Seek-R1
2) The dataset is described as covering diverse scenes, yet all footage is collected within a single campus. This might undermine claims about solving scene diversity and generalization.
3) In Appendix A.2, the authors describe a three-annotator protocol for temporal labeling but provide no inter-annotator agreement statistics or disagreement resolution analysis. Without metrics such as agreement rate, the quality, consistency, and potential bias in temporal labels remain unclear. In other words, how often did they agree/disagree. And how often during disagreement did number three go with number 1 or number 2.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The full dataset viewer is not available

additional_feedback.value:
1) Include quantitative comparisons with at least one aerial anomaly detection baseline 
2) Report agreement statistics across annotators (e.g., overall and per class), frequency of disagreement.

final_justification.value: The authors provided a clear and thorough rebuttal that addressed all major concerns. They added comparisons with aerial-specific baselines (HSTforU, ANDT), clarified the dataset’s diversity and generalization protocol, and reported strong annotation agreement. The dataset viewer issue was also resolved. These additions strengthen both the empirical and methodological claims of the paper. I am now confident in its contributions and have updated my score to 5.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper introduces the first large-scale benchmark for aerial video anomaly understanding. It fills the gap in this field and shows diversity in anomaly types, scenarios and weather conditions, making it a valuable contribution.
2. The proposed method A2Seek-R1 adopts a two-stage pipeline, combining Graph-of-Thought (GoT) supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement fine-tuning. This design improves both reasoning ability and spatial localization.
3. The paper introduces a novel seeking mechanism that allows the model to actively propose regions for further inspection. This enhances the model’s spatial awareness in complex aerial scenes.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The concept of Graph-of-Thought (GoT) is not clearly explained. Specifically: (i) Why is GoT preferred over Chain-of-Thought (CoT) or video descriptions for supervised fine-tuning? (ii) How is GoT implemented in practice? Figure 1(e) and Appendix C are somewhat abstract. A concrete GoT annotation example and a clearer explanation in the method section would help.
2. While the paper focuses on spatial grounding and frame-level reasoning, it lacks discussion or evaluation on temporal localization (i.e., identifying when an anomaly occurs). How are key frames selected, and how does the method handle long-duration anomalies (e.g., running or loitering)?
3. The evaluation metric in Table 2 is not clearly described. A dedicated paragraph explaining the metrics for different tasks (e.g., reasoning, localization) would improve clarity.
4. There are minor typos (e.g., repeated "Second" in Line 85; extra “)” in Line 108) that should be corrected.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The authors provide a complete, well-structured, and user-friendly dataset, but the related implementation code has not been released.

final_justification.value:
This work makes two major contributions:
1. It introduces the first comprehensive Aerial Anomaly Detection dataset, filling an important gap in the field.
2. It proposes A2Seek-R1, a method that leverages Graph-of-Thought and reinforcement learning to enhance reasoning performance for the task.

In the rebuttal, the authors have effectively addressed the key concerns:
1. They clarified the implementation details of Graph-of-Thought and demonstrated its effectiveness for reasoning through solid experiments.
2. They resolved the concerns regarding dataset diversity and model generalization.

Overall, the experiments are solid, the methodology is innovative, and the effort to collect a realistic and high-quality dataset is commendable. By the way, I expect the authors to further improve the writing of the paper in future revisions. Therefore, my final recommendation is: Accept.

title.value: A2Seek: Towards Reasoning-Centric Benchmark for Aerial Anomaly Understanding

TLDR.value: We introduce A2Seek, a reasoning-centric benchmark for aerial anomaly understanding, and A2Seek-R1, a method designed to seek and interpret anomalies.

abstract.value:
While unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer wide-area, high-altitude coverage for anomaly detection, they face challenges such as dynamic viewpoints, scale variations, and complex scenes. Existing datasets and methods, mainly designed for fixed ground-level views, struggle to adapt to these conditions, leading to significant performance drops in drone-view scenarios.
To bridge this gap, we introduce A2Seek (Aerial Anomaly Seek), a large-scale, reasoning-centric benchmark dataset for aerial anomaly understanding. This dataset covers various scenarios and environmental conditions, providing high-resolution real-world aerial videos with detailed annotations, including anomaly categories, frame-level timestamps, region-level bounding boxes, and natural language explanations for causal reasoning. 
Building on this dataset, we propose A2Seek-R1, a novel reasoning framework that generalizes R1-style strategies to aerial anomaly understanding, enabling a deeper understanding of “Where” anomalies occur and “Why” they happen in aerial frames.
To this end, A2Seek-R1 first employs a graph-of-thought (GoT)-guided supervised fine-tuning approach to activate the model's latent reasoning capabilities on A2Seek. Then, we introduce Aerial Group Relative Policy Optimization (A-GRPO) to design rule-based reward functions tailored to aerial scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a novel “seeking” mechanism that simulates UAV flight behavior by directing the model's attention to informative regions.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that A2Seek-R1 achieves up to a 22.04\% improvement in AP for prediction accuracy and a 13.9\% gain in mIoU for anomaly localization, exhibiting strong generalization across complex environments and out-of-distribution scenarios. Our dataset and code are released at https://2-mo.github.io/A2Seek/.

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
